title: Encounter and Change
bigQuestion: When Europeans and Native peoples met, what changed for each of them, and who got to tell the story?

story.title: Furs and Kettles on the River
story.kicker: In the winter of 1680, a French trader and an Illinois family met on the Illinois River, and each of them wanted something the other had.
paragraphs: The canoe scrapes onto the frozen mud near where Peoria stands today. A Frenchman named Pierre climbs out, stamping his cold feet. He has paddled from the north with three companions. In his canoe are iron kettles, steel knives, glass beads, wool blankets and a musket. He has come to trade. Up the bank is a village of the Illinois people, hundreds of long houses covered with woven mats.

A man named Chicagou walks down to meet him with his wife, Keewatin, and their son. They have met French traders before. Chicagou carries beaver pelts, soft and thick from the winter. Beaver fur is worth a lot in Paris, where hat makers pay silver for it. Pierre knows this. Chicagou knows Pierre knows it. They begin to talk, half in French, half in the Illinois language, with a lot of hand signs.

Keewatin wants the kettle. Her clay pots crack in the fire and take days to make. An iron kettle lasts for years. Chicagou wants the knife and the musket. A steel blade cuts faster than stone. A musket can kill a deer from far away, and it can frighten an enemy. Pierre wants as many beaver pelts as he can carry. They argue politely for an hour. In the end, both sides walk away pleased.

That evening Pierre eats corn and venison in the family's house. He has learned to smoke the long pipe that the Illinois offer to guests. It means peace. He tells them that a French leader named La Salle is building a fort nearby. Chicagou nods. More French means more kettles. It might also mean more of the sickness that has emptied some villages. He does not say this out loud.

Pierre and Chicagou are made-up names, but this trade really happened, thousands of times, all along the rivers of Illinois. The French wrote about it in their letters and journals. The Illinois told about it in their own stories. Both sides gained, and both sides lost. That is the story of this chapter.
story.think: Pierre and Chicagou both walked away happy. What might each of them lose in the years ahead that they could not see on that day?

lessons.title: Spices, Gold and God
lessons.mainIdea: Europeans in the 1400s wanted a sea route to Asia for trade, and they also wanted gold, land and converts to their religion.
reading: In the 1400s a pinch of pepper in Europe was worth more than its weight in silver. Pepper, cinnamon and cloves came from Asia. So did silk. The goods traveled thousands of miles by land, and every merchant along the way raised the price. European kings and merchants wanted a cheaper way. They wanted to sail to Asia and buy the *spices* directly.

Portugal tried first. Its sailors crept down the coast of Africa, year after year. In 1488 a Portuguese captain rounded the southern tip of Africa. In 1498 another reached India by sea. Spain, Portugal's rival, wanted its own route. A sailor from Italy named Christopher Columbus had an idea. He would sail west, across the ocean, and reach Asia from the other side.

Trade was not the only reason. Europeans also wanted gold, because gold was money. They wanted land, because land made a family rich. And many wanted to spread their religion, *Christianity*. Priests sailed with the soldiers. One historian summed up the reasons as gold, God and glory. All three were on the ships that sailed west.

words.d: plant products like pepper and cinnamon used to flavor food, very costly in Europe
the religion of most Europeans, which many wanted to spread to new lands

look.title: The Price of Pepper
look.text: A sack of pepper leaves India on a ship. It is unloaded and carried by camel across a desert. It is sold to a new merchant in a city on the Mediterranean Sea. Then it is shipped to Italy, and sold again. Then it goes over the mountains to Germany. At every step, someone adds a fee. By the time a cook in Germany buys a pinch, it costs twenty times what it cost in India.
look.prompt: If you could sail straight from Europe to India and skip all those middle steps, what would happen to the price? Who would gain and who would lose?

check.q: Why were spices so expensive in Europe?
choices: They were carried a long way and sold many times
check.why: Spices came from Asia over long routes, and each merchant along the way raised the price.

check.q: What was Columbus's idea?
choices: To sail west across the ocean to reach Asia
check.why: Columbus believed Asia was not far to the west and that he could reach it by sailing across the Atlantic.

check.q: Which was NOT one of the main reasons Europeans sailed west?
choices: To find a cheaper route for trade
check.why: The reasons were trade, gold, land and religion. Learning Native languages was not a goal.

lessons.title: What 1492 Set in Motion
lessons.mainIdea: Columbus landed in the Caribbean in 1492 believing he had reached Asia, and his voyage started centuries of contact that changed both worlds.
reading: On October 12, 1492, after about five weeks at sea, three Spanish ships reached a small island in the Bahamas. Columbus went ashore and claimed it for the king and queen of Spain. The people who lived there, the *Taíno*, came out to meet the strangers. Columbus thought he had reached islands near India. So he called the people Indians. The name stuck, though it was a mistake.

Columbus wrote in his journal that the Taíno were gentle and generous. They brought parrots, cotton thread and food. In the same pages, he wrote that they would make good servants and could be easily ruled. He took some Taíno back to Spain by force. On later trips, the Spanish made Taíno people dig for gold. Within a few decades, war, hunger and disease had killed most of the Taíno on the islands.

Columbus never reached Asia and never understood that he had found continents unknown to Europe. But his voyage changed history. Ships began to cross the Atlantic every year. Plants, animals, people, ideas and diseases moved in both directions. Historians call this the *Columbian Exchange*. The next lessons show what it carried.

words.d: the people who lived on the islands of the Caribbean when Columbus arrived
the movement of plants, animals, people and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world after 1492

look.title: Columbus Writes About the Taíno
look.text: In his journal for October 1492, Columbus described the people he met as friendly and eager to trade. He wrote that they gave whatever they had and asked for little. He also wrote that they had no iron weapons, and that with a small number of armed men he could take control of them all and make them do whatever he wished.
look.cite: Journal of Christopher Columbus, October 1492 (paraphrased from later copies)
look.prompt: Columbus praised the Taíno and, in the same breath, planned to rule them. What does this tell you about how he saw them?

check.q: Why did Columbus call the people he met Indians?
choices: He thought he was near India
It was the name of the island
check.why: Columbus believed he had reached islands near India in Asia, so he used that name.

check.q: What happened to most of the Taíno within a few decades?
choices: They died from war, hunger and disease
check.why: Forced labor, war and new diseases killed most of the Taíno on the islands.

check.q: What is the Columbian Exchange?
choices: The movement of plants, animals, people and diseases across the Atlantic after 1492
A trade between Columbus and the king
check.why: After 1492, living things moved in both directions between the Americas and the rest of the world.

lessons.title: Corn Goes East, Wheat Goes West
lessons.mainIdea: Foods from the Americas fed the world, and animals and crops from Europe changed the Americas.
reading: Look at a pizza. The wheat crust and the cheese came from Europe. The tomato sauce came from the Americas. Before 1492, no one in Italy had ever seen a *tomato*. No one in Ireland had seen a potato. No one in Africa had grown corn. No one in Mexico had eaten a cow or tasted wheat bread. The Columbian Exchange put them all on one plate.

Native farmers had bred corn, potatoes, tomatoes, peppers, beans, squash, peanuts, cacao for chocolate and many more plants over thousands of years. Once these crossed the ocean, they fed millions. Potatoes grow well in cold, poor soil, so they became the main food of Ireland and northern Europe. Corn spread across Africa and China. The population of the world grew partly because of American crops.

Going the other way came wheat, rice, sugar cane, coffee, bananas and fruit trees. Also animals: cattle, pigs, sheep, goats, chickens and horses. The Americas had no large farm animals before this except the llama. Pigs and cattle ran wild and multiplied. They also trampled Native cornfields. Sugar cane grew so well in the Caribbean that Europeans built huge farms, and soon they were bringing enslaved Africans by force to work them.

words.d: a plant first grown in the Americas that became a key food in Europe after 1492
a tall grass grown for sugar, brought to the Americas and grown on large farms with enslaved labor

look.title: Two Dinner Tables in 1491
look.text: In a village in Italy, a family eats bread, cheese, cabbage and a little pork. There is no tomato, no potato, no corn, no chocolate. In a village in Mexico, a family eats corn tortillas, beans, squash, peppers and turkey. There is no beef, no wheat, no cheese, no sugar, no rice.
look.prompt: Pick one food you ate this week. Was it from the Americas, from the rest of the world, or a mix? Could you have eaten it in 1491 where you live?

check.q: Which food came from the Americas to Europe?
check.why: Potatoes were bred by farmers in South America and became a main food in Europe.

check.q: Why did potatoes become so important in Ireland?
choices: They grow well in cold, poor soil
The Spanish forced people to eat them
check.why: Potatoes give a lot of food from small, cold fields, which fit northern Europe.

check.q: What was one harmful effect of sugar cane in the Caribbean?
choices: Europeans brought enslaved Africans by force to grow it
It made the islands too sweet
check.why: Sugar farms needed huge amounts of labor, and Europeans met it with enslaved people taken from Africa.

lessons.title: The Horse Changes the Plains
lessons.mainIdea: Horses brought by the Spanish spread north and turned Plains peoples into fast-moving hunters and riders within about two hundred years.
reading: There were no horses in the Americas when Columbus landed. The Spanish brought them to Mexico in 1519. Native people had never seen anything like them. Some Spanish soldiers on horseback seemed at first to be one giant animal. But soon Native peoples learned to ride, and they learned fast. Horses escaped or were traded, and they spread north across the land.

For Plains peoples, the horse was a revolution. Before, a family could carry only what their dogs could pull. Hunting bison on foot was slow and dangerous. On horseback, a hunter could ride into a herd and pick the animal he wanted. Tipis grew bigger, because horses could haul longer poles. Families could move farther and faster. Nations like the Comanche and Lakota became some of the best riders in the world.

The horse also brought conflict. Nations moved onto the Plains that had never lived there before. They competed for hunting grounds and for horses. Raids to take horses became common. By the 1700s, before most Plains people had ever met a white settler, their lives had already been changed by a European animal. That is how the Columbian Exchange worked: its effects ran ahead of the Europeans themselves.

words.d: a change so big that it turns a way of life upside down
a Plains nation famous for its skill with horses in the 1700s and 1800s

look.title: The Horse Moves North
rows: Pueblo Revolt frees thousands of horses
Comanche riding on the southern Plains, about
Lakota riding on the northern Plains, about
look.cite: Standard dates used by historians of the Plains, rounded
look.prompt: About how long did it take horses to travel from Mexico to the northern Plains? How did they get there without Spanish riders?

check.q: Where did the horses of the Plains come from?
choices: They came north from the Spanish in Mexico
The English brought them to the Plains
check.why: The Spanish brought horses to Mexico in 1519, and they spread north by escape and trade.

check.q: How did horses change bison hunting?
choices: Riders could pick out an animal and chase it
Horses scared the bison away for good
check.why: Riding into a herd was far faster and safer than hunting on foot.

check.q: What does it mean that the Exchange 'ran ahead of the Europeans'?
choices: Plains life changed because of horses before most Plains people met Europeans
check.why: Horses spread across the Plains by the 1700s, long before white settlers arrived there.

lessons.title: Sickness Crosses the Sea
lessons.mainIdea: Diseases from Europe killed more Native people than any war, because no one in the Americas had ever been exposed to them.
reading: The deadliest thing on the European ships was invisible. It was *germs*. Smallpox, measles and the flu had lived in Europe, Asia and Africa for thousands of years. People there often caught them as children. Many died. Many others survived. A survivor could not catch the disease again. That is called *immunity*. No one in the Americas had ever met these germs. No one had immunity.

When smallpox reached a Native village, nearly everyone got sick at the same time. There was no one healthy to bring water or food. In 1520, smallpox reached the great Aztec city of Tenochtitlan in Mexico. It killed the emperor and a large share of the people. The Spanish captured the weakened city the next year. Disease did more to defeat the Aztecs than Spanish steel.

Sickness spread along trade routes faster than Europeans traveled. Some villages lost most of their people before they ever saw a European. Historians do not agree on exact numbers. But they agree that a very large share of Native people died in the two centuries after 1492. It was one of the greatest losses of life in human history. The survivors rebuilt. But their world was smaller, and their nations were weaker when the settlers came.

words.d: tiny living things that cause disease and spread from person to person
the body's ability to fight off a disease it has met before

look.title: A Village After the Sickness
look.text: A French priest walks into a village on a river in the 1600s. Last year it held five hundred people. Now the corn stands unharvested. Many houses are empty. The people left are mostly old and very young. An elder tells him that the sickness came from traders upriver, before any Frenchman had set foot here.
look.prompt: How could a disease reach a village before any European did? What would this do to a nation's ability to defend its land?

check.q: Why did European diseases kill so many Native people?
choices: Native people had never met these germs and had no immunity
The diseases were new in Europe too
check.why: Immunity comes from having met a germ before. No one in the Americas had, so nearly everyone got sick at once.

check.q: What helped the Spanish capture Tenochtitlan in 1521?
choices: Smallpox had killed a large share of the city's people
check.why: Smallpox reached the city in 1520 and killed the emperor and many others, weakening it before the Spanish attack.

check.q: Why could a village lose people to disease before meeting any European?
choices: The disease came through the air from Europe
Germs spread along Native trade routes
The disease came from the bison
check.why: Traders carried germs from village to village along routes that were already old.

lessons.title: Spanish Soldiers and Missions
lessons.mainIdea: The Spanish conquered Native empires, forced people to work and built missions to change their religion, and in 1680 the Pueblo people drove them out.
reading: The Spanish came first and came to rule. In 1519 a soldier named Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico with a few hundred men. He had horses, steel, guns and smallpox on his side. He also had thousands of Native allies who hated the Aztecs. He captured Tenochtitlan in 1521. Spain took the Aztec gold and silver and ruled Mexico for three hundred years. Spanish soldiers who conquered are called *conquistadors*.

In the lands they took, the Spanish gave Native villages to Spanish settlers. The villagers had to work for the settler and pay him. Priests built *missions*, churches with farms around them. Native people were required to live there, work and become Christians. Some priests protected the people from the worst abuse. Many did not. Native religions were banned, and ceremonies were punished.

The Pueblo peoples of New Mexico put up with this for about eighty years. Then in 1680, a religious leader named Popé sent runners to every pueblo with knotted cords. The knots counted the days until the uprising. On the chosen day the pueblos rose together. They killed hundreds of Spanish and drove the rest out of New Mexico. The Spanish did not return for twelve years. No other Native uprising against Europeans in what is now the United States was so successful.

words.d: a Spanish soldier who conquered lands in the Americas in the 1500s
a church and farm where priests required Native people to live, work and become Christians
the 1680 uprising in which the Pueblo peoples drove the Spanish out of New Mexico

look.title: The Knotted Cord
look.text: A runner arrives at a pueblo out of breath. He hands the leader a cord of yucca fiber with several knots. Each morning the leader unties one knot. When the last knot is gone, every pueblo across New Mexico will rise on the same day. The runner speaks a different language from this pueblo, but the knots need no words.
look.prompt: Why did Popé use knotted cords instead of a written message? What problems did he solve by having every pueblo act on the same day?

check.q: What helped Cortés capture Tenochtitlan besides horses and guns?
choices: The Aztecs surrendered without a fight
Smallpox and thousands of Native allies
check.why: Disease weakened the city, and Native nations who hated Aztec rule joined the Spanish.

check.q: What was a mission?
choices: A church and farm where Native people were made to live, work and become Christians
check.why: Missions combined a church with farms and required Native people to change their religion and work there.

check.q: What happened in the Pueblo Revolt of 1680?
choices: The Pueblo peoples drove the Spanish out for twelve years
check.why: Led by Popé, the pueblos rose together and pushed the Spanish out of New Mexico until 1692.

lessons.title: French Traders on the Rivers
lessons.mainIdea: The French came in small numbers to trade furs, so they relied on Native alliances, learned Native languages and often married into Native families, including in Illinois.
reading: The French did things differently. Few French people wanted to move across the ocean. Those who came wanted beaver fur, which sold for high prices in Europe for hats. To get fur, they needed Native hunters. So the French built trading posts, not big farms. They learned Native languages. Many French traders married Native women. Their children grew up in both worlds.

In 1673 a priest named Jacques Marquette and a trader named Louis Jolliet came down the Mississippi. They were paddling canoes. They were the first French to see Illinois. The Illinois people welcomed them with the *calumet*, a long peace pipe. On the way home they went up the Illinois River. They passed a village of thousands near where Utica is today. Marquette wrote that the land was rich and the people kind.

Soon French forts and missions dotted the rivers. La Salle built a fort near Peoria in 1680. The town of Kaskaskia in southern Illinois started as a French mission in 1703. Illinois hunters brought furs, and French traders brought kettles, cloth, guns and brandy. The French also brought disease. They drew the Illinois into wars against the Iroquois and others. But French and Native people in Illinois lived side by side for nearly a century. Many families were both.

words.d: the exchange of animal furs, especially beaver, for European goods like kettles and cloth
a long decorated pipe smoked to show peace and friendship

look.title: Marquette Meets the Illinois
look.text: In his journal, Marquette wrote that when he and Jolliet came to a village of the Illinois in 1673, an elder came out to greet them with his hands raised toward the sun. The elder said that the sun was beautiful because the French had come to visit, and he invited them into the village in peace. They were given a feast and a calumet to carry as a sign of safe passage.
look.cite: Jacques Marquette, journal of the 1673 voyage (paraphrased from a later printed version)
look.prompt: This is the French side of the meeting. What might an Illinois elder have written about the same day, if he had kept a journal?

check.q: Why did the French need Native allies more than the Spanish did?
choices: The French did not want land
Few French came, and they depended on Native hunters for furs
check.why: The fur trade only worked with Native hunters, so the French built alliances instead of conquering.

check.q: Who were the first French to see Illinois?
check.why: Marquette and Jolliet paddled down the Mississippi and up the Illinois River in 1673.

check.q: What was the calumet?
choices: A peace pipe offered to guests
check.why: The long pipe was smoked to show peace, and carrying one gave safe passage among nations.

lessons.title: English Farms and Fences
lessons.mainIdea: The English came as families to farm, so they took more land than the Spanish or French, and land became the main cause of war.
reading: The English came last and came to stay. Jamestown in Virginia began in 1607. Plymouth in Massachusetts began in 1620. Unlike the French, English settlers came by the thousands, as whole families. They wanted farms of their own. They cleared forests, built fences and let cattle and pigs roam. Every new farm was land that a Native nation had used for hunting, fishing or planting.

At first, Native nations helped. The Powhatan people traded corn to starving Jamestown. The Wampanoag leader Massasoit made a treaty with Plymouth and shared a harvest feast with them in 1621. But the English kept coming. The two sides also thought about land differently. To Native peoples, land was shared by a nation for use. To the English, land was *property* that one person owned and could fence and sell.

Within fifty years the friendship broke. In 1675 Massasoit's son Metacom, called King Philip by the English, led many nations against the settlers. The war burned dozens of towns on both sides. Thousands died. The English won, and Metacom was killed. After that, the pattern in English lands was set: settlers moved in, the *frontier* moved west, and Native nations were pushed off the land.

words.d: something owned by one person, who can fence it, keep others out or sell it
the edge of the land settled by Europeans, which kept moving west

look.title: Who Settled Where, and When
rows: Spanish found Santa Fe, New Mexico
look.prompt: Put the three countries in order of who arrived first in what is now the United States. Which reached Illinois?

check.q: How were English settlers different from French traders?
choices: The English came as farming families and took much more land
The English came in small numbers
The English married into Native families more often
check.why: Thousands of English families came to farm, and each farm meant land taken from a Native nation.

check.q: How did the English and Native peoples see land differently?
choices: The English shared land; Native nations sold it
Native nations shared land for use; the English saw it as property to own and sell
check.why: This difference led to endless misunderstanding and conflict about what a land deal meant.

check.q: Who was Metacom?
choices: Massasoit's son, who led a war against the English in 1675
check.why: The English called him King Philip. His war was the last big attempt to push the English out of New England.

sections.title: Loss, Resistance and Points of View

lessons.title: Land Lost, Lives Lost
lessons.mainIdea: Over three centuries, Native nations lost most of their land and many of their people through disease, war and treaties, including here in Illinois.
reading: Add it up. Disease killed a very large share of Native people. Wars killed more. Then came *treaties*, written agreements between a Native nation and a government. On paper, a treaty was a deal between equals. In practice, nations weakened by sickness and war often had no better choice. So they signed. Many treaties were broken as soon as settlers wanted more land.

Illinois shows the whole story. When Marquette came in 1673, the Illinois people numbered many thousands in big villages. Disease and wars with other nations shrank them. In 1803 the Kaskaskia, one of the Illinois nations, signed a treaty giving up most of their land to the United States. The Sauk leader Black Hawk tried to return to his village on the Rock River in 1832. Soldiers and militia drove his people out in a short, brutal war.

In 1833 a treaty was signed in Chicago. In it the Potawatomi gave up their remaining land in northern Illinois. Within a few years they were marched west. By the 1840s almost no Native nation held land in Illinois. The state was named for a people who were no longer allowed to live in it. That was the cost of the encounter. The people who were here first paid it.

words.d: a written agreement between a Native nation and a government, often about land
ordinary citizens who serve as part-time soldiers

look.title: Black Hawk Remembers the Rock River
look.text: In the story of his life, told in 1833 after his defeat, Black Hawk said that the land along the Rock River was a beautiful country. He said he loved his town, his cornfields and the home of his people, and that he had fought for it. He asked what people would think of a man who did not fight for the place where his family was buried.
look.cite: Black Hawk, Life of Black Hawk, told to an interpreter, 1833 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Black Hawk was defeated, yet he was asked to tell his story and it was printed. Why might it matter that his side was written down at all?

check.q: What is a treaty?
choices: A written agreement between a nation and a government
check.why: Treaties were the legal way land passed from Native nations to the United States, though many were unfair or broken.

check.q: Why did weakened nations often sign treaties giving up land?
choices: The treaties gave them more land
They had little choice after disease and war
check.why: Nations shrunk by sickness and fighting could not hold off settlers and often signed to survive.

check.q: What happened to the Potawatomi after the 1833 treaty in Chicago?
choices: They were marched west within a few years
They moved to Canada and returned
check.why: The treaty gave up their remaining land in northern Illinois, and they were removed west.

lessons.title: Resisting and Adapting
lessons.mainIdea: Native peoples fought back, made alliances, took up new tools and kept their languages and ceremonies alive, and they are still doing so.
reading: Native nations were never just victims. They chose, planned and fought. The Pueblo Revolt of 1680 drove out an empire. Metacom nearly did the same in New England. In 1763 an Ottawa leader named Pontiac united nations around the Great Lakes and captured most of the British forts west of the mountains. Illinois nations joined him. The British had to promise that settlers would stay east of the mountains, though the promise was soon broken.

Nations also adapted, which means changing to fit new conditions. They took the horse and became the finest riders on Earth. They took iron, guns and cloth and made them their own. Some nations played the French, Spanish and English against each other to protect their land. Native leaders learned to read treaties and argue in court. Adapting was not giving up. It was survival.

The hardest thing to protect was *culture*: language, ceremony, story. Governments and missions worked for centuries to stamp these out. Yet the Haudenosaunee still hold council. The Hopi still plant corn the old way. Native languages are being taught again to children in Illinois and across the country. The Illinois language itself, called Miami-Illinois, is being relearned from old French dictionaries. Resistance did not end. It changed shape.

words.d: to change how you live so you can survive new conditions
a people's language, beliefs, ceremonies, stories and ways of living

look.title: A Word Comes Back
look.text: In a classroom in the 2000s, a girl practices a word from the Miami-Illinois language. Her great-great-grandparents spoke it every day. Then it stopped being spoken. Now a scholar has rebuilt the language from dictionaries that French priests wrote three hundred years ago. The girl says the word for river out loud. It has not been spoken in that room for a very long time.
look.prompt: Why might a language matter so much to a nation? How is learning it again a kind of resistance?

check.q: What did Pontiac do in 1763?
choices: United Great Lakes nations and captured most British forts in the west
check.why: Pontiac's alliance took most British forts west of the mountains and forced a promise to hold back settlers.

check.q: Which is an example of adapting?
choices: Refusing to ever use metal tools
Learning to ride horses and read treaties
check.why: Adapting means taking new tools and skills to survive, not giving up who you are.

check.q: How is the Miami-Illinois language being relearned?
choices: From dictionaries written by French priests long ago
check.why: French priests in the 1700s wrote down the language, and scholars are using those pages to bring it back.

lessons.title: Same Event, Different Stories
lessons.mainIdea: The same event looks different depending on who tells it, so good historians read more than one side and ask who wrote a source and why.
reading: Here is one event. In 1621 Wampanoag men and English settlers at Plymouth ate together after the harvest. For many Americans, this is the first Thanksgiving, a happy story of sharing. For many Wampanoag today, the same day is the start of a story that ends with their land taken and their nation nearly destroyed. Both are talking about the same meal. Both are telling the truth about part of it.

That is why a *point of view* matters. A point of view is the position a person sees from. A Spanish soldier, a Spanish priest, an Aztec warrior and an Aztec farmer would each describe the fall of Tenochtitlan differently. Most written records from this time were made by Europeans. Native accounts were spoken, painted or remembered. To hear them, historians have to look harder.

Good readers ask three questions about any *source*. Who made it? When? Why? Columbus wrote his journal to impress the king and queen who paid for his trip. Black Hawk told his story to explain himself after losing a war. Neither one is lying, but each has a reason to tell it his way. Today some places mark the second Monday of October as Columbus Day, and others call it Indigenous Peoples' Day. That argument is about which story we choose to remember.

words.d: the position a person sees an event from, which shapes how they describe it
a record from the past, such as a journal, letter, painting or spoken story

look.title: Two Reports of One Trade
look.text: A French trader writes home: 'Today I traded one kettle and two knives for twelve fine beaver pelts. A very good bargain.' The same evening an Illinois hunter tells his family: 'Today I traded twelve pelts, which took me all winter, for a kettle that will last my wife ten years and knives that will feed us. A very good bargain.'
look.prompt: Both think they won. Is one of them wrong? What could a historian learn by reading both accounts instead of one?

check.q: Why do the Wampanoag and many other Americans tell the 1621 harvest feast differently?
choices: One side is making it up
They are describing the same event from different points of view
check.why: Both describe a real meal, but what happened afterward shapes how each side remembers it.

check.q: Why are there fewer written Native accounts from this time?
choices: Native people had nothing to say
Native accounts were mostly spoken, painted or remembered, not written
Native people wrote only in Spanish
check.why: Most Native nations kept history by oral tradition and art, so historians must look beyond written pages.

check.q: What three questions should you ask about a source?
choices: Is it long, is it old, is it famous?
Is it true, is it false, is it fun?
Who made it, when, and why?
Where is it kept, who owns it, how much is it worth?
check.why: Knowing the maker, the time and the purpose tells you what point of view shaped the source.

review.q: What was the main reason Europeans first wanted a sea route to Asia?
choices: To buy spices and silk more cheaply
review.why: Asian goods were very costly after passing through many merchants, and a direct route would cut the price.

review.q: Which of these traveled from the Americas to the rest of the world?
review.why: American crops fed the world. Horses, cattle, wheat, sugar and the diseases came the other way.

review.q: Which killed the most Native people after 1492?
review.why: Native people had no immunity, and epidemics killed a very large share of the population.

review.q: Which country relied most on fur trade and Native alliances?
review.why: Few French came, and they depended on Native hunters for the beaver furs they wanted.

review.q: Why did the English take more Native land than the French?
choices: English families came by the thousands to farm
review.why: Each new farm took land that a Native nation had used, and English settlers kept coming.

review.q: What did the Pueblo Revolt and Pontiac's war have in common?
choices: Both were led by the Spanish
Both were Native nations uniting to push Europeans out
Both ended with treaties in Chicago
review.why: In 1680 and 1763, many communities acted together to drive out or hold back a European power.

review.q: What happened to Native nations in Illinois by the 1840s?
choices: They had signed treaties and been removed west
They had joined the state government
They had grown to their largest size
review.why: Treaties in 1803 and 1833, and the Black Hawk War of 1832, ended with almost no Native land left in Illinois.

review.q: Why should a historian read both Columbus's journal and a Native account of 1492?
choices: Because Native accounts are always correct
Because each shows a different point of view on the same event
review.why: Every source has a maker, a time and a purpose, and comparing sources gives a fuller picture.
